title: Staying between
hookLine: walking between traditions asks for extra respect: tag the source, don't borrow the sacred carelessly; Tertullian and Augustine argue it out
tomorrow: Abraham threw a guest out of his tent. what happened next?

lines: WHAT HAS ATHENS TO DO WITH JERUSALEM?
cards: A playlist called calm: a chant from a monastery, a Sufi song, a singing bowl, none of them labeled. Borrowing is easy now. Early Christian writers argued over it.

Tertullian, a sharp-tongued writer from Carthage, put the question in a line, here in an old public-domain English translation: "What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" Athens meant the philosophers.
Jerusalem meant the faith. His answer: nothing at all.

teach.b: Tertullian's case at its strongest: mixing sources blurs them. He saw the heresies of his day growing out of philosophy, and wanted the faith kept plain.
Pour the philosophers into the faith and you get something that is neither. Keep them apart, so each stays itself. Augustine saw it another way, and he used a story to say it.
When Israel left Egypt, Exodus says, "they borrowed of the Egyptians jewels of silver, and jewels of gold," and carried them out.
Augustine read that as permission: whatever is true and good in the philosophers belongs to God, so take it and put it to good use. But notice how he takes it.

He doesn't hide where it came from: he names the philosophers, the Platonists above all, and says their gold was God's all along, scattered everywhere. Both views sit in the Christian library, and each has its heirs.
For someone walking between traditions, they make a fair pair of rules. From Augustine: you may carry what's true from one house to another, and say where you found it.
From Tertullian: don't blend it into mush, and don't use the sacred as decoration. Put together, that's today's practice: tag the source.
A mantra, a candle, a mala: each has a home. Say where it comes from, what it means there, and who keeps it.

how: Christian thinkers debated how to use learning from outside the faith, from Tertullian's 'Athens and Jerusalem' to Augustine's 'gold of Egypt'. On a personal path drawn from many sources, each borrowed practice is named with its source, its meaning there and the people who keep it.

o: walking among traditions without joining one, with extra care
mixing every tradition into one new religion of your own
switching to a new tradition every year or so

games.q: Athens and Jerusalem: tap the pairs.
p: what has Athens to do with Jerusalem?
take Egypt's gold, and use it well
jewels of silver and jewels of gold

s: Tertullian asked what Athens has to do with Jerusalem
"what indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" his answer: nothing.
Augustine said Christians should never use the philosophers' ideas
he read Egypt's gold as truth that may be carried out and put to good use.
once you own a sacred object, its meaning is up to you
on this path a borrowed thing keeps its home: tag the source.

games.q: you side with Augustine: take what's true wherever you find it. now state Tertullian's case at its strongest.
o: mixing blurs the faith until it isn't itself; keep them apart and keep it plain.
philosophy is always wrong, so nothing outside the faith is worth knowing.
borrowing is fine as long as nobody notices where it came from.
games.why: Tertullian's best case is clarity: he saw heresies growing out of philosophy, and blending loses what made the faith itself. Augustine answered by naming where he found it.

practice: Look at one thing near you that came from a tradition not your own: a candle, a bead, a word you use, a song. Ask it three questions in silence: where are you from, what do you mean there, and who keeps you?
If you can't answer, that's the borrowing to check.
